top.title: Changing the antibiotic playbook to catch an ESKAPE artist
top.summary: Nearly a century ago, a single colony of Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus) helped launch the antibiotic age. In 1928, Alexander Fleming returned to his London lab to find that a stray mold had wiped out the Staphylococcus growing on one of his plates. The accident gave the world penicillin, ushering in the age of biomedicine and ensuring that an infected cut or scrape would not be fatal.

top.title: A child's first 5 years set them up for life. African study explores how to target education spending

top.title: From strays to territory bosses: Epigenetics makes cheetahs adaptable
top.summary: The findings of a new study led by the Leibniz-IZW on Namibian free-ranging cheetahs (Acinonyx jubatus jubatus) demonstrate that epigenetic mechanisms might play an important role in how animals develop different phenotypes despite their low genetic diversity. The work is published in the journal Molecular Ecology.

top.title: Deep biosphere has endured mountain-building and erosion over hundreds of millions of years
top.summary: A new study reveals that microbial life deep within Earth has persisted and repeatedly flourished through hundreds of millions of years of mountain-building and erosion. By analyzing minerals, fluids and gases from a 2.3-kilometer-deep (1.4-mile-deep) borehole in central Sweden, researchers have uncovered episodic bursts of methane-producing life linked to major geological events that shaped Scandinavia.

top.title: Weak hydrogen bonds dethrone copper as the most stable metal binder, opening a new path for metal selection
top.summary: Copper has been knocked off the top of a stability ranking it had dominated for decades. Without altering the atoms directly bonded to the metal, a KAIST research team reversed the longstanding trend in which copper generally forms the most stable complexes by tuning only the weak hydrogen bonds in its surrounding environment.

more.title: 'The Jungle Book' offers an unconventional tool for undergraduate economics education
more.summary: Research in the International Journal of Pluralism and Economics Education argues that "The Jungle Book" can serve as an unconventional teaching tool for undergraduate economics, using the original stories by Rudyard Kipling as well as Disney film adaptations to introduce concepts ranging from scarcity and sustainability to happiness and development.

more.title: Inexpensive blue pigment enables efficient one-step conversion of carbon dioxide to methane
more.summary: A common blue pigment could help turn carbon dioxide (CO₂) from an industrial waste product into a useful fuel. A joint research team led by Tohoku University's Advanced Institute for Materials Research (WPI-AIMR), in collaboration with Hokkaido University and startup AZUL Energy, has developed a catalyst that converts CO₂ directly into methane (CH₄) with high efficiency using copper phthalocyanine, an inexpensive…

more.title: Port Hills research reveals 'fire trap' risk from non-native grass
more.summary: New research from Te Whare Wānanga o Waitaha | University of Canterbury (UC) examining the aftermath of the February 2024 Port Hills wildfire found that some young native trees and shrubs were able to resprout after being badly damaged by fire.

more.title: Ships, ice cores and krill surveys underpin Australia's 10-year Antarctic monitoring strategy
more.summary: The important role ships play in gathering scientific data in Antarctica and the Southern Ocean has been outlined at a leading Antarctic science conference in Hobart. The biennial Australian Antarctic Research Conference was held at the University of Tasmania and attracted 400 researchers from around the globe.

more.title: 'Heel-strike' may have allowed early humans to walk farther—at the cost of high-impact forces
more.summary: The average person takes thousands of steps each day, instinctively walking heel-to-toe. Although they hardly register them, those consistent heel-first strides are more distinctive to humans than previously thought and allowed early hominins to walk farther and more efficiently, but at the cost of higher impact forces on bones and joints, according to a new study led by a researcher at Penn State.

more.title: How climate change may amplify the impact of earthquakes in the Arctic
more.summary: Permafrost refers to permanently frozen ground. The rock is held together by ice, much like cement binds concrete. However, when the ice thaws, the ground becomes weak and unstable. During an earthquake, this can trigger a series of natural hazards. An international research team investigated precisely such an event.

more.title: Neutrophil vesicles help Candida albicans evade immune-cell engulfment
more.summary: The immune system is a highly sophisticated defense network designed to protect against pathogens. A research team from the Universities of Würzburg and Jena and the Leibniz Institute for Natural Product Research and Infection Biology (Leibniz-HKI) has shown that certain components of the immune system can actually help the yeast Candida albicans evade immune attack.

more.title: Workshops Educate African Researchers On How to Publish With IEEE
more.author: Kathy Pretz
more.summary: Many researchers and students in Kenya, Rwanda, and Uganda struggle to access and publish scientific and technical articles because of financial barriers including publishing fees and subscriptions to research libraries. To help, IEEE has made its Xplore Digital Library more accessible by offering discounts on subscriptions and lowering fees to publish articles.

more.title: How beavers can help create fire breaks as part of a drought preparation plan
more.summary: Most of the countryside around the Holnicote estate in Somerset has been dry and dusty for most of the summer. But one corner remains conspicuously green.

more.title: Early Earth's auroral belts may have formed a natural ion-beam reactor for prebiotic chemistry
more.summary: We usually think of auroras as beautiful lights in the night sky. I see them as visible traces of a connection between the sun, Earth's magnetic field and the atmosphere. This led me to an origin-of-life question: Could the planetary structure that produces auroras also have organized chemical reactions on early Earth?

more.title: How Indigenous Protected Areas became a vital way to protect nature in Australia
more.summary: When you think of conservation in Australia, chances are you'll think of a national park.

more.title: Park rangers and residents speak up to save Togo's last national park
more.summary: A few years ago, I drove with an old friend from Togo, West Africa, towards the country's last remaining large protected area, Fazao-Malfakassa National Park. Our destination was the Hotel Fazao, where his uncle had once worked as a professional chef after its opening in 1980.

more.title: AI governance model inspired by Pope Leo XIV aims to put ethics first
more.summary: Researchers at the John Paul II Catholic University of Lublin (KUL) and the University of Eastern Finland have developed a new model of artificial intelligence governance inspired by the teachings of Pope Leo XIV as set out in his encyclical Magnifica Humanitas. The new model is intended to ensure that AI technologies are developed and used safely, fairly and with full respect for human rights.

more.title: War drama Pressure depicts D‑day's weather forecast—what we found when we recreated the challenge using modern systems
more.summary: Meteorologist James Stagg gave what many regard as the most important weather forecast in history in June 1944. The fate of more than 150,000 Allied troops preparing to invade the Normandy beaches on D-Day and the future of the war in Europe depended on Stagg and his forecasting teams. Get the forecast wrong and an already perilous invasion might not succeed, prolonging the war.

more.title: The listening gap is real—how AI might help teachers bridge it
more.summary: A Grade 4 teacher showed her class a video of children who walk miles barefoot to school. A hand shot up: "Why are you showing us AI slop? No way this is real."

more.title: Why 'you're smart' can backfire: Young children may cheat more after ability praise
more.summary: Parents and teachers might think telling kids "they're smart" is a helpful way to build self-confidence and support positive development.

more.title: New nitride semiconductor expands material options for more powerful electronics
more.summary: Polar wurtzite nitride semiconductors, such as aluminum nitride (AlN) and gallium nitride (GaN), are central to modern high-power and high-frequency electronic devices because of their wide band gaps, high breakdown electric fields, and strong spontaneous and piezoelectric polarization.

more.title: Stripped-down LSD reveals structural features linked to hallucinogenic and therapeutic effects
more.summary: University of California, Davis, researchers have stripped down LSD to the base features responsible for its hallucinogenic and therapeutic effects.

more.title: What can a pair of underpants tell you about your vegetable garden?
more.summary: This summer, 115 participants in Leiden and The Hague worked with scientists from Leiden University to investigate the soil life in their community garden plots. With mangetout peas, a taste test, a buried pair of underpants and a harvest festival, they helped scientists better understand the connection between soil, plants and people.

more.title: Slender crystal's blue-to-yellow glow could make invisible forces visible
more.summary: Applying pressure to luminescent organic crystals usually brings molecules closer together and weakens their fluorescence. Materials that instead brighten and undergo a large color change are rare, and clear design principles for achieving both responses in simple, rigid aromatic hydrocarbons have been lacking.

more.title: Yes, passing 1.5 C of global warming is cause for alarm, but not despair
more.summary: The news has been full of headlines about findings from a United Nations report: The world is set to exceed the 1.5°C global warming target set out in the 2015 Paris Agreement. The report has raised concerns and questions about what a 1.5°C increase could mean for our world.

more.title: New report offers lessons for preserving cultural heritage in crisis zones
more.summary: The report, "Digital heritage preservation for vulnerable collections: Reflections on the Sudan Memory project history and inventory," was authored by Dr. Laura Gibson, senior lecturer in digital content management education at King's, alongside Sara El-Nager, independent researcher and editor, and Dr. Hannah Ishmael, lecturer in digital culture & race.

more.title: Reversible electric control unlocks persistent chiral phonon states
more.summary: Atoms in a material are rarely still. They jiggle back and forth in collective lattice vibrations known as phonons. Their motion can also carry a rotational element: In 2023, scientists at PSI experimentally proved the existence of chiral phonons, which exhibit handedness depending on which way they rotate.
